newsitem.title: CHINA: China cautious on use of force in islands row.
newsitem.headline: China cautious on use of force in islands row.

text.p: China said on Tuesday it would take a cautious approach to the idea of sending naval forces to a group of disputed islands in the East China Sea.
Anti-Japanese activists in China, Taiwan and Hong Kong have been demanding tough military action over the islands, known as the Diaoyus in Chinese and the Senkakus in Japanese.

"The situation around the Diaoyu islands is relatively complicated. On sending ships there, we feel there is a need for caution," Foreign Ministry Spokesman Shen Guofang told a news briefing in Beijing.
A simmering dispute over the uninhabited by potentially resource-rich islands flared in July when a right-wing Japanese group landed on one of the group and built a lighthouse there.
The islands are claimed by Beijing, Tokyo and Taipei and outrage over Japan's refusal to tear down the makeshift lighthouse has united traditional foes China and Taiwan under a banner of nationalism.
Activists in China, Hong Kong and Taiwan have joined in calling on Beijing to send warships to the area.
Shen said Japan bore a certain responsibility to resolve the dispute and urged Tokyo to take quick action to prevent further harm to relations between the two countries.
"The Japanese should take measures as soon as possible to... prevent a recurrence of similar matters," he said.
Shen dismissed reports that Chinese authorities had forced prominent anti-Japanese activist Tong Zeng to leave Beijing, saying he had left the city to conduct research.
"According to our understanding, he went out of Beijing to do his own specialised technological research," Shen said.
Friends of Tong have said Chinese officials told him to leave Beijing on Sunday on a business trip after he tried to organise a protest against Tokyo's control over the islands.
Shen said China allowed protests provided they took place within the law. "Democratic demonstrations will be approved if they are based on the law," he added.
Tong's vocal anti-Japanese campaigns led authorities to confiscate his passport and exile him temporarily from Beijing during the U.N.-sponsored World Conference on Women last year.
